Carl Henry
karl HEN-ree
proper noun (an evangelical theologian)
Carl Ferdinand Howard Henry (1913-2003), American evangelical theologian, founding editor of Christianity Today, and author of God, Revelation and Authority.

Biblical Definition

Carl F. H. Henry (1913-2003) was an American evangelical theologian, journalist, and churchman, a leading architect of the mid-twentieth-century “new evangelicalism,” the founding editor of Christianity Today, and the author of the massive six-volume work God, Revelation and Authority, a sustained defence of the rationality of the Christian faith and the authority of God's propositional revelation in Scripture. The dictionary honours much in Henry's labour. Against the prevailing liberalism and neo-orthodoxy of his day, he defended the inspiration, inerrancy, and propositional truth of Scripture—that God has spoken truly and intelligibly, that the prophecy came not by the will of man but as holy men were moved by the Holy Ghost, that God's word is true from the beginning and shall stand for ever. He labored to give evangelicalism intellectual seriousness and to recall it to social as well as personal responsibility without surrendering the gospel. His high doctrine of Scripture and his defence of revealed truth against the irrationalism of neo-orthodoxy are a genuine service to the church. The dictionary, holding the Reformed and confessional faith, notes its differences and cautions. Henry was a broad evangelical, not a confessional Reformed theologian, and the “new evangelicalism” he helped lead, for all its strengths, opened doors—through its instinct for cultural engagement and cooperation—that later admitted the very compromises it meant to resist, as the trajectory of some of its institutions showed. The dictionary applies its rule: honour the genuine good—Henry's defence of biblical inerrancy and revealed, propositional truth, his intellectual seriousness, his stand against liberalism and neo-orthodoxy—while reading his broad-evangelical program through the corrective of the confessional Reformed tradition, which roots the defence of Scripture in the whole system of doctrine the great confessions set forth.

CARL HENRY, proper noun. Carl F. H. Henry (1913-2003), American evangelical theologian.

Founding editor of Christianity Today and architect of the “new evangelicalism.”

Author of the six-volume God, Revelation and Authority.

Defended the inspiration, inerrancy, and propositional truth of Scripture against liberalism.

Honoured for his stand for revealed truth, read through the confessional Reformed corrective.

Key Scripture

2 Pe 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Ps 119:160 — "Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever."

Mt 5:18 — "For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Isa 40:8 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the caution is that the “new evangelicalism” Henry helped lead, for all its strengths, opened doors of cultural cooperation that later admitted the compromises it meant to resist.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours much in Carl Henry. Against the liberalism and neo-orthodoxy that dominated the academy of his day, he defended the inspiration, inerrancy, and propositional truth of Scripture—that God has spoken truly and intelligibly, that prophecy came not by the will of man but as holy men were moved by the Holy Ghost, that God's word is true from the beginning and shall stand for ever. His six-volume God, Revelation and Authority is a monument of the defence of revealed truth against irrationalism, and he labored to give evangelicalism intellectual seriousness and a recovered sense of social responsibility without surrendering the gospel. This is genuine service to the church.

Yet the dictionary, holding the confessional Reformed faith, marks its differences and cautions without disparaging the man. Henry was a broad evangelical, not a confessional Reformed theologian, and the “new evangelicalism” he helped lead, for all its strengths, carried an instinct for cultural engagement and cooperation that later opened doors to the very compromises it meant to resist, as the drift of some of its institutions showed. The dictionary applies its rule: honour the genuine good—Henry's defence of inerrancy and revealed truth, his stand against liberalism—while reading his broad-evangelical program through the corrective of the confessional tradition, which roots the defence of Scripture not in a minimal evangelicalism but in the whole system of doctrine the great Reformed confessions set forth.
